analysis.one_liner: Bolsters copyright and trademark enforcement with bigger damages, stiffer criminal penalties, and a new White House enforcement office.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 410-11 on May 8, 2008, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never voted before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would expand federal copyright and trademark enforcement: it doubles the minimum and maximum statutory damages for trademark counterfeiting, extends triple damages to more cases, makes exporting infringing goods a violation, adds new criminal forfeiture and restitution rules, and directs the Sentencing Commission to consider stiffer sentences for exporting pirated goods. It would also create a new White House intellectual property enforcement office, post 10 additional U.S. intellectual property attaches in foreign embassies, add FBI agents and prosecutors to 'CHIP' units, and authorize $25 million a year in grants to state and local police to enforce intellectual property laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Record labels, movie studios, and trademark-holding manufacturers gain the most: higher damage awards, new forfeiture of equipment and proceeds, expanded federal and local enforcement dedicated to their rights, and dedicated diplomats abroad to press their claims. Individual performers gain a small restitution and customs-notification provision for bootleg recordings. Consumers of goods like medicines and auto parts gain indirectly from stronger action against dangerous counterfeits.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the minimum and maximum statutory damages for trademark counterfeiting, from $500-$100,000 per mark to $1,000-$200,000, and the top for willful cases from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000.

Extends mandatory treble (triple) damages to cases of intentionally inducing counterfeiting or supplying goods and services knowing they will be used in a counterfeit operation, and adds prejudgment interest.
Makes exporting infringing copies and counterfeit-marked goods a violation, matching the existing import ban.

Adds new criminal and civil forfeiture of equipment, proceeds, and facilitation property for copyright and counterfeit-label offenses, drug-law-style, plus mandatory restitution to copyright and trademark owners.
Adds penalties of up to 20 years' imprisonment for knowingly or recklessly causing serious bodily injury, and any term up to life for causing death, in counterfeit-goods trafficking cases.

Creates the Office of the United States Intellectual Property Enforcement Representative in the Executive Office of the President to write a recurring Joint Strategic Plan and coordinate all federal IP enforcement.

Directs the Patent and Trademark Office to appoint at least 10 additional intellectual property attaches in U.S. embassies and the Attorney General to deploy 5 additional overseas IP law enforcement coordinators.
Expands FBI and Justice Department staffing: at least 2 FBI agents and 1 assistant U.S. attorney per CHIP unit, 10 new CHIP districts, and a 5-agent headquarters unit for international cases.

Authorizes $25 million a year (fiscal 2008-2012) in grants to state and local police for overtime, equipment, and task forces to enforce intellectual property laws, and adds online copyright infringement to existing computer-crime grants.
Gives performers restitution for unauthorized recordings of live musical performances and lets them pay a fee to be notified by Customs of importations of such recordings.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the new White House office, embassy attaches, overseas coordinators, additional FBI agents and prosecutors, and the local police grant program. Defendants in IP cases face a much higher damage ceiling, easier treble damages, expanded forfeiture of property connected to a case, and a federal push to prosecute more cases. Ordinary consumers also bear the downstream effects of stronger enforcement built around industry claims, such as higher costs for goods and a more aggressive posture toward online sharing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and defendants in IP cases

drawbacks.text: The bill ratchets up the machinery of the copyright and trademark industries: a White House enforcement office, dedicated diplomats, more FBI agents, and local police grants for enforcing IP claims. Enforcement of private property rights in intellectual works would be carried out largely at public expense.
Mandatory treble damages and doubled statutory damages shift power toward large rights-holders, who can better afford to litigate; the $1,000 per-mark minimum applies even where actual harm is small.
Expanded civil forfeiture of any property 'used or intended to be used' in an offense extends drug-war-style asset seizure to intellectual property cases.

The good-faith case for the bill is real: counterfeit goods can be genuinely dangerous, and the bill adds up-to-20-years and life-imprisonment penalties for counterfeit trafficking that causes serious injury or death. An honest supporter would weigh that safety benefit against the cost of a larger enforcement apparatus.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety provisions against dangerous counterfeits (fake medicines, auto parts) are the strongest public-interest argument, and the restitution provisions help individual performers. But the bill's center of gravity is a large expansion of remedies and enforcement capacity for the largest copyright and trademark holders, financed by taxpayers, with little in the bill directly protecting consumers' own interests in cases that do not involve health and safety.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it overwhelmingly under a suspension-of-the-rules vote that only needed a two-thirds majority, but after the Senate received it on May 12, 2008 it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and that Congress ended with no Senate action.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee held hearings in December 2007, amended the bill in subcommittee in March 2008, and reported it by voice vote on May 5, 2008.

The House passed the bill on a motion to suspend the rules (a streamlined procedure with limited debate needing a two-thirds majority) by a recorded vote of 410-11: 224-4 among House Democrats and 186-7 among House Republicans.
The Senate received the bill on May 12, 2008 and referred it to the Senate Judiciary Committee; the record shows no further action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As recorded, no one fully won: the media and trademark industries secured a lopsided House endorsement and momentum, but the Senate never acted, so no new penalties or enforcement machinery took effect through this bill and taxpayers were spared its costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Content and trademark industries in momentum; no new law

for.name: John Conyers, Jr.
for.role: House Judiciary Committee Chairman; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired the committee that amended and reported it, and managed its floor passage under suspension of the rules.

for.name: Motion Picture Association and recording industry
for.role: Content industry groups backing stronger anti-piracy enforcement
for.what_they_did: Publicly promoted the bill as a crackdown on counterfeiting and piracy that would expand federal enforcement of their rights.

against.name: 11 House members who voted no
against.role: 7 Republicans and 4 Democrats voting against passage
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, the only recorded opposition in either chamber.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred on May 12, 2008
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral; it never reached a Senate vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan: House Democrats voted 224-4 for passage and House Republicans 186-7 (410-11 overall).

industries.note: The bill's higher damage ceilings, easier treble damages, forfeiture of equipment and proceeds, expanded FBI and prosecutor staffing, and dedicated White House and embassy enforcement all strengthen the copyright holders' hand, largely at public expense. Their gain comes through stronger legal power over how ordinary people access and share media.

industries.industry: Trademark-holding manufacturers (consumer goods, pharmaceuticals, auto parts)
industries.note: Doubled statutory damages, broadened treble damages, the export ban, and new criminal penalties for injury or death from counterfeits all favor established brands. Here the industry's interest partly runs with the public's: dangerous counterfeit medicines and parts are a genuine consumer-safety problem.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: IP-TIC grants (up to $25 million a year) would reimburse police overtime, storage, equipment, and task forces for enforcing intellectual property laws. New public resources would be directed toward private rights enforcement.

The bill adds restitution for bootleg live recordings and a paid customs-notification service for unauthorized importations. This is one provision whose beneficiary is working artists rather than large studios.
